opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core question is about the returns to research effort. The usual way to frame it is: if you double the cumulative input going into algorithmic research, whether that's researchers, their time, or eventually AI systems doing the work, how much do you improve the efficiency of your algorithms? If each doubling of research input more than doubles algorithmic efficiency, then once AI systems are doing the research, you get a loop where better algorithms make more capable or more numerous AI researchers, which then produce better algorithms faster. That's the setup for something like a software-only intelligence explosion.

The tricky part is that ideas tend to get harder to find. We see this across many fields, where sustaining a constant rate of progress requires exponentially growing research effort. So the real question is whether the returns are steep enough to overcome that diminishing-returns effect. When people try to estimate this from historical data, in areas like computer vision, language modeling, or other software domains, the estimates often land in a range that's uncomfortably close to the threshold. It's not obvious that we're clearly above or clearly below the point where the feedback loop would accelerate rather than fizzle out.

I'd add a couple of important caveats. First, a lot of algorithmic progress doesn't come purely from thinking harder. It comes from running experiments, and experiments need compute. If compute is a key complementary input, then even if you have a huge number of automated researchers, you may be bottlenecked by the experimental compute you have. That can substantially dampen the feedback loop, because the compute stock doesn't grow just because your researchers got smarter. Second, a fair amount of what we measure as algorithmic progress is itself driven by scale. Some innovations only become useful or discoverable at larger compute budgets, so separating algorithmic progress from hardware scaling is harder than it looks.

So my overall take is that I'm fairly uncertain. I don't think the evidence rules out an accelerating loop, but I'm skeptical of strong claims that software alone will take off extremely quickly. I tend to think the more likely picture is that automated AI research speeds things up meaningfully, but that it stays tied to growth in compute and the broader economy, so you get faster progress rather than a sudden discontinuity. Still, given how close the estimates are to the critical threshold, I think it's a scenario we should take seriously and try to measure much more carefully.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I think about it is that this is fundamentally a question about elasticities. You have some amount of research effort going into improving algorithms, and the question is: if you double the inputs, how much do you increase the rate of algorithmic progress? And then separately, how much does that progress feed back into making the next round of research cheaper or more effective?

At Epoch we've tried to measure the first piece empirically. If you look at things like ImageNet, or language modeling, or other benchmarks where we have a long enough time series, you can decompose the gains into the part that comes from scaling compute and the part that comes from better algorithms. And what we find is that algorithmic progress has been quite substantial — roughly on the order of halving the compute needed to reach a given level of performance every eight months or so for language models, though there's a lot of uncertainty on that number. So the historical rate is fast, but it's also been driven by a growing pool of researchers and a growing amount of compute to run experiments on. It's not obvious how much of it is "ideas" versus "ideas enabled by having a lot more hardware to try things on."

That's the crux for the feedback-loop question. If you automate AI research, you can potentially expand the effective research workforce very quickly — much faster than you could by training humans. But if the binding constraint is experimental compute rather than cognitive labor, then adding a hundred thousand automated researchers doesn't help as much as the naive story suggests, because they're all queuing for the same GPUs. So I'd want to know the returns to cognitive labor holding compute fixed. My own guess is that there are real returns there — a lot of what researchers do is not running giant experiments, it's figuring out which experiments are worth running, debugging, finding bugs in the data pipeline, and so on — but they're probably diminishing, and you'd eventually run into a compute wall.

The other thing I'd look at is whether the returns to research are themselves declining as the field matures. In most areas of science and technology we see something like ideas getting harder to find: each successive improvement takes more effort than the last. If that's true in AI as well, then you need the automation to be sufficiently strong to outpace that decline for the loop to actually accelerate rather than just sustain itself. My read of the evidence is that this is plausible but not guaranteed — the research-effort elasticity we estimate is high enough that a large expansion of effective researchers could produce an acceleration for some period, but I'd put real probability on it fizzling out as compute and diminishing returns start to bite. I'd rather frame it as "a boost of some magnitude for some duration" than a binary question of whether there's an explosion.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish two questions. One is whether AI can automate a substantial fraction of AI research. The other is whether doing so creates a feedback loop that actually accelerates. You can have the first without the second, because research might become harder as you make progress.

The key thing I’d want to estimate is how much algorithmic improvement you get from an additional unit of research effort. Then I’d ask how much that improvement increases the amount of effective research you can do. Better algorithms might let you run more AI researchers with the same compute, or make each researcher more capable. Those gains feed back into the next round of research.

But there are countervailing forces. Discovering the next improvement might require substantially more work. Experiments take time and compute. And an AI that’s good at writing code isn’t necessarily equally good at choosing promising research directions or interpreting an unexpected result.

So evidence that algorithms are improving quickly is relevant, but it doesn’t by itself establish an accelerating feedback loop. You need to understand the relationship between research inputs and improvements, and how those improvements translate into further research capacity. I’d look for evidence that increasingly capable systems can deliver sustained, end-to-end research gains under realistic resource constraints. That would be much more informative than success on isolated research tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish algorithmic progress from the feedback loop itself. We can observe that better algorithms let us achieve a given level of performance with less compute. But that doesn’t, by itself, tell us whether automating AI research will produce an accelerating process.

For that, you need to understand how research output responds to additional research effort. Suppose AI systems make researchers twice as productive. How much algorithmic improvement does that generate? And how much does that improvement increase the productivity of the next generation of AI researchers? Those are the links that determine whether the loop accelerates.

One possibility is that ideas become harder to find, so you need increasingly large amounts of research effort to sustain the same rate of progress. Automation could offset that without producing a dramatic acceleration. Another possibility is that improvements make automated research sufficiently cheaper and more capable that the additional research effort outpaces those diminishing returns.

I’d want to look at evidence on both sides: historical algorithmic improvements relative to the resources devoted to research, and experiments measuring how effectively AI systems can carry out research tasks. Crucially, those tasks should involve producing useful improvements, rather than just solving problems with known answers.

And then there are bottlenecks. You might generate ideas very quickly but still need substantial compute and time to test them. So the question isn’t simply whether AI can improve its own algorithms. It’s whether those improvements expand effective research capacity fast enough, across the whole research process, to sustain an acceleration.
